title: Fortis and Takeda Launch 'Mission Dengue Free India' Awareness Campaign
excerpt: The nationwide initiative pairs physician-led community sessions with digital outreach to tackle a disease that officially struck over 113,000 Indians in 2025.
body:
• Fortis Healthcare and Takeda India have launched "Mission Dengue Free India," a nationwide education and prevention initiative aimed at curbing the country's recurring dengue burden.
  • The campaign will run physician-led sessions at selected Fortis hospitals, resident welfare associations, schools, colleges and companies, alongside public talks, doctor articles, podcasts and digital resources.
  • India reported more than 113,000 officially recorded dengue cases in 2025, with health officials acknowledging the true burden is higher.
  • The initiative follows a WHO-aligned integrated approach — combining education, vector control, timely diagnosis and case management — and was facilitated by Mitsui & Co.

Fortis Healthcare and Takeda India have launched "Mission Dengue Free India," a nationwide awareness and prevention campaign targeting one of the country's most persistent public-health threats.

The initiative combines physician-led education sessions at selected Fortis hospitals, residential associations, schools, colleges and corporate workplaces with public talks, doctor-written articles, video podcasts, social media outreach and digital resources. The hospital network will also roll out dedicated dengue-awareness programmes in its own facilities during the high-risk dengue season.

Why now

The timing is seasonal — and strategic. Dengue cases in India surge with the monsoon, and the numbers remain formidable: more than 113,000 cases were officially reported in 2025, according to data from the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control, with experts noting the actual burden is significantly higher due to underreporting.

Dengue's pattern is cruelly predictable. Stagnant water in and around homes breeds the Aedes aegypti mosquito, the bite is often painless and unnoticed, and the fever it causes can escalate within days into severe dengue — a medical emergency defined by plasma leakage, severe bleeding or organ impairment.

What the campaign does

The campaign's backbone is direct community engagement. Fortis physicians will lead awareness sessions designed to help people recognise early symptoms, eliminate mosquito breeding sites and seek timely diagnosis and care — the single biggest lever against severe outcomes.

"India faces a significant dengue burden that continues to affect millions of lives and overwhelm healthcare systems, with the true extent likely underreported. Mission Dengue Free India is our shared commitment to change this reality."

— Vinayak, AVP – Marketing, Fortis Healthcare

Vinayak said the initiative aims to build a "well-informed, resilient and dengue-free India" by empowering communities with knowledge and motivating sustained preventive action — from clearing waterlogged containers at home to recognising warning signs that demand immediate hospital care.

The partners behind it

The collaboration pairs one of India's largest private hospital networks with the Indian arm of the Japanese pharmaceutical major, and was facilitated by Mitsui & Co., whose healthcare business portfolio spans hospitals, pharmaceuticals and medical equipment.

For Takeda, the campaign sits alongside its broader dengue work in the country. "A healthier and more resilient future depends on action today — whether that's controlling vectors, improving early diagnosis, ensuring effective case management, or advancing prevention through vaccination where aligned with national recommendations," said Ted Kim, President of Takeda India. He added that the mission "brings this integrated vision to life — supporting India's public health goals and aligning with WHO's call for comprehensive, community-driven dengue control."

What you can do

The campaign's core message is practical. Empty or cover water storage containers weekly, clear roof gutters and discarded tyres, use repellents and screens during peak mosquito hours, and treat high fever with body aches, rash or pain behind the eyes during dengue season as a reason to get tested promptly — not a reason to wait.

For the diaspora, the campaign is timely for another reason: the dengue season overlaps with the winter travel window when many NRIs visit family in India. Checking local outbreak conditions before a trip, packing repellent and knowing the symptoms can make the difference between a routine visit and a medical emergency.
